structure.rationale: The book follows the split the requester specified: Part 1 (The Plan 9 Model) lays down the three composing pillars — files as the uniform resource interface, 9P as the single protocol that reaches them, and the per-process namespace that assembles them into a program's view — using the 'Plan 9 from Bell Labs' overview paper as the grounding source, with no history or biography. Part 2 then walks outward from the same three pillars in dependency order: Namespaces (the abstraction itself) before 9P Protocol (the wire mechanism namespaces are built from) before File Servers (the things namespaces name and 9P talks to); Mount, Bind, and Union Directories follow as the operators that construct a namespace from those servers; Process Namespaces then shows how that construction interacts with rfork/process lifecycle; Plumbing is placed next as a worked example of the whole model — an ordinary file server used as an interprocess bus; and Security and the Capability Model closes the book, since Plan 9's security design (no setuid, factotum, capabilities) is best understood as a consequence of everything established before it — namespace restriction standing in for privilege. Each concept builds strictly on the ones before it, so a reader who proceeds in order never meets an unexplained mechanism.
structure.audience: Technically savvy readers already comfortable with systems programming and Unix-family OS concepts, who want Plan 9's actual design and mechanisms — not its history — explained precisely.

claims.text: Plan 9's design rests on three composing ideas: resources are named and accessed like files in a hierarchical file system; a single protocol, 9P, is used to access those resources whether they are local or remote; and the disjoint hierarchies exposed by different services are joined by the client into one private hierarchical name space.

Plan 9 applies the file/directory metaphor far more broadly than traditional Unix: windows, network connections, running processes, the mouse, the graphics device, and remote machines' resources are all represented as files or directory trees that are opened, read, written, and closed with the same small set of operations, rather than through separate special-case system calls (ioctl, socket options, and the like).

9P is the one protocol used to reach every resource in the system: the kernel speaks it to serve local devices, and the identical protocol is used over a network connection to talk to a file server on another machine, so a remote resource is reached exactly the same way as a local one.

Every process has its own private name space — its own view of the file hierarchy — rather than sharing one global file tree; a name space is assembled by binding and mounting resource trees (served locally by the kernel or remotely by a 9P server) at chosen points.

Because a name space is just a client-side composition of file trees reached over 9P, building a custom view of the system requires no new system calls or kernel support for each new kind of resource — adding a resource to your world is a bind or mount, not a new API.

The window system, 8½, is itself an ordinary file server: it serves files such as /dev/cons and /dev/bitblt, and gives each window client a distinct copy of those files in that window's own local name space, so the same path name (e.g. /dev/cons) resolves to a different underlying resource depending on whose name space is doing the resolving.

Conventional path names (such as /net, /dev, /proc, /bin) are consistent across every Plan 9 machine, but what is actually bound or mounted underneath those names — and therefore what a program actually finds there — can differ per process and per machine; a program always knows where to look, not necessarily what it will find.

Some conventional directories are union directories — a single directory backed by several component directories bound together and searched in order — used, for example, so that /bin resolves to the right set of executables for the current architecture without a program needing to know which one is active.

Network access is exposed as a file hierarchy under /net: a protocol directory (e.g. /net/tcp) contains a clone file used to reserve a new connection (reading it returns a connection number), and each numbered connection directory exposes ctl and data files — writing a connect command to ctl establishes the connection, and data carries the bytes — so dialing out is ordinary file I/O rather than a socket system call.

9P governs whole file systems, not individual files in isolation: it includes the procedures to resolve names and walk the hierarchy the server exports, and it operates at the level of bytes rather than fixed blocks — a deliberate difference from block-oriented network file protocols such as NFS. The client's assembled name space is held entirely on the client side, never on or shared with the server, which is itself a departure from name-space designs like Sprite's.

Plan 9's own overview paper frames the payoff with a naming analogy: 'my house' and a house's precise postal address name the same place, but the informal phrase is easier to say, means something only in context, and changes meaning depending on who says it — exactly how a Plan 9 path such as /dev/cons or /bin/date is a conventional, context-dependent name, while what actually answers it is local and can legitimately differ from process to process and machine to machine.

The window system 8½ demonstrates the three pillars composing into distribution transparency: each window is created with its own private name space, so a program running in a remote window still just opens /dev/mouse, /dev/bitblt, and /dev/cons as usual — it 'does not know whether the files are local,' because the 9P connection to the file server providing them is already established and multiplexed into that window's namespace before the program ever runs.

pitfalls: Readers from a Unix background tend to assume a bind or mount is a global, persistent change (like editing /etc or adding a symlink). In Plan 9 it changes only the acting process's name space (and any process that shares it) — the same bind performed in one window is invisible from another window's shell unless the name space is explicitly shared or the change is made before the fork that separated them.

"Everything is a file" in Plan 9 is easy to under-read as just Unix's version of the same slogan. Plan 9 pushes further: Unix still special-cases sockets, ioctls, and many device controls outside the ordinary file interface, whereas Plan 9 routes control operations themselves (e.g. dialing a network connection, above) through plain opens/reads/writes on ctl and data files, which is what lets one protocol (9P) and one client interface cover them all.

The three pillars are easy to state as a checklist and easy to under-appreciate as a system: the payoff is specifically that they compose — file-naming (pillar 1) is what makes one protocol sufficient (pillar 2), and one protocol is what makes client-side name-space assembly (pillar 3) possible without kernel changes for every new resource type. Explaining any one pillar in isolation, without the composition, misses the actual design contribution.

A 'uniform global name space' is not the same claim as Plan 9's design, and conflating them is a common misreading. Plan 9 explicitly does not give everyone the same tree; it gives everyone the same conventional path names (/dev/cons, /bin/date, /net) resolved against a locally assembled namespace, so the guarantee is 'a program always knows where to look,' not 'every machine sees identical contents there.'

claims.text: A name space is a per-process attribute: a single rooted hierarchy of file names, assembled by binding and mounting service trees at chosen points. Unlike a conventional kernel's one global, shared file tree, Plan 9 has no such tree at all — every process's view is its own, and the file server itself never sees or holds the assembled result, only its own local hierarchy.

bind(char *name, char *old, int flag) grafts a file or directory already visible somewhere in the current name space onto another point (old) in that same name space. It requires no server communication and no open connection — it only rearranges names already reachable. The evaluation of name happens at bind time, not on each later lookup through old, so a later change to what name resolves to does not retroactively change old.

mount(int fd, int afd, char *old, int flag, char *aname) attaches the entire file tree served over an already-open, already-connected file descriptor fd (a pipe or network connection to a 9P server) so that its root appears at old. A kernel file-system type called the mount device is the sole bridge between the ordinary procedural interface user code sees (open/read/write/close) and the RPC messages that actually cross the wire to the server — the mount device does the marshaling and multiplexing, and it's the only integral RPC mechanism in Plan 9.

Both bind and mount take a flag governing how new content joins whatever is already at old: the default (MREPL) replaces old outright; MBEFORE/MAFTER instead add the new directory to the front or back of a union directory, searched in that order; MCREATE additionally marks a unioned directory as eligible to receive files a later create places there. (The full mechanics of union lookup, creation, and unmount are covered in the next chapter, Mount, Bind, and Union Directories — this chapter only needs that the two operators exist and what they attach.)

A name space's propagation across process creation is controlled explicitly, not implied by a single fork() semantics: plain fork() (equivalent to rfork(RFFDG|RFREND|RFPROC)) shares the parent's name space with the child — they become two processes pointing at one name space object, so a bind or mount performed by either is immediately visible to the other. rfork(RFNAMEG) instead gives the child a private copy, identical at the instant of the call but independent thereafter. rfork(RFCNAMEG) gives the child a wholly empty name space that must be built from nothing by mounting an open file descriptor onto it (RFNAMEG and RFCNAMEG are mutually exclusive).

Because a shared name space is literally one object referenced by multiple processes rather than copies kept in sync, the precise term for a set of processes sharing a name space this way is a name-space group — bind(2)/mount(2)'s own description defines their scope as 'the current process and other processes in its name space group.' RFNOMNT additionally can be set on a new name space to forbid further mounts and dereferencing of kernel-device names beginning with '#' inside it — useful for building a deliberately restricted namespace (relevant later for the security model).

A Plan 9 process's name space is not built from an empty root by hand each time: init(8) constructs the initial one from a namespace(6) description file, interpreted by the newns/addns library routines. Each line is one operation — mount, bind, import, cd, unmount, clear (rfork(RFCNAMEG), i.e. start over empty), or '.  path' to include another such file — using the same option letters (-a/-b/-c/-C) as the bind(1)/mount(1) commands. Every later bind or mount a running process performs builds on top of that starting point; the description file is a bootstrap, not a permanent record.

ns(1) prints a live process's actual name space (by default the caller's own, or a given pid's) as a script of bind/mount/import commands that could, in principle, reconstruct it — derived by reading and reformatting /proc/pid/ns. It is the closest thing Plan 9 offers to a name-space inspector, and by default it also rewrites raw /net/tcp/N/data paths back into readable network addresses.

Name-space construction is what buys customization without new mechanism: binaries for a given CPU architecture live in an architecture-named directory (e.g. /mips/bin), and each machine binds the one it needs to the conventional name /bin; a directory of a user's private binaries is typically unioned in ahead of it. The Plan 9 shell, rc, has no PATH variable at all — the 'which directories hold runnable commands' problem that Unix solves per-shell-instance with an environment variable is instead solved once, structurally, by the name space itself.

Name-space construction is what buys transparency: the window system, 8½, is an ordinary 9P server for files such as /dev/cons, /dev/mouse, and /dev/bitblt; each window gets its own private copies of those names bound into its own name space. A client program addressing /dev/cons has no way to ask, and no need to know, whether that window (and therefore that file) is being served locally or by a machine across the network — the same mechanism plumbed through import lets Plan 9 run X11 as an ordinary 8½ client with a measured ~10% graphics performance cost over a bare local Plan 9 machine.

Name-space construction is what makes most special-case system calls disappear: process control that Unix spreads across kill(2), ptrace(2), and assorted /proc conventions is, on Plan 9, plain text I/O on files under /proc/pid — writing 'kill' or 'stop' to ctl, reading status for state, reading/writing mem for a debugger, writing note to deliver a signal-like note. The command ps is close to a reformatted cat /proc/*/status; a debugger opens /proc/pid/text and /proc/pid/mem directly, with no ptrace-equivalent call anywhere.

import host [remotepath] mountpoint extends a local name space across a network at no special-purpose cost: it dials the remote machine, starts a 9P server there for the requested subtree, calls mount to attach that connection locally, then exits — leaving the remote process to keep serving. Concrete uses from the source paper: importing a remote floppy drive (import lab.pc /a: /n/dos) and importing a remote /proc for cross-machine debugging (import helix /proc; db /proc/27/text /proc/27/mem), the latter working across CPU architectures because db reads the target's byte order from the executable header on the text file rather than assuming its own.

The cpu command builds an entirely new name space on a remote CPU server by re-importing the pieces of the terminal's local name space that the shell needs (terminal-resident devices), while CPU-local resources such as the fast local file system connection stay local — so working 'on' the CPU server feels like the local processor simply got faster, not like moving to a different login session. The paper contrasts this explicitly with rlogin, which moves the user into a wholly distinct remote name space, and with NFS, which keeps one uniform name space but forces execution to stay on the client.

snippets.note: Exact signatures from bind(2)/mount(2)/unmount(2); flag is one of MREPL, MBEFORE, MAFTER, optionally OR'd with MCREATE (mount also has MCACHE).

snippets.code:
rfork(RFFDG|RFREND|RFPROC)   // == plain fork(): shares the name space with the parent
rfork(RFNAMEG |RFPROC)       // child gets a private COPY of the parent's name space
rfork(RFCNAMEG|RFPROC)       // child starts with an EMPTY name space
snippets.note: fork(2) is literally defined as this rfork() call; RFNAMEG and RFCNAMEG are mutually exclusive.

bind -a /root/386/bin /bin
bind -a /root/rc/bin  /bin
bind '#c' /dev
cd /usr/glenda

snippets.code:
cat /proc/*/status                # a crude ps
echo stop >/proc/17/ctl           # suspend process 17 — no ptrace() call
db /proc/27/text /proc/27/mem     # attach a debugger — local or, via import, remote
snippets.note: Process control as plain file I/O under /proc, replacing kill/ptrace/wait-family special calls.

pitfalls: It's tempting to assume rfork's name-space handling defaults to 'copy,' matching how fork() behaves for memory in most systems. Plan 9's plain fork() actually SHARES the name space object outright — RFNAMEG is the flag that copies it. Forgetting this is a real source of bugs: a bind performed in what you thought was an isolated child is visible everywhere else in the same name-space group, because there was never a separate copy to isolate it.

MREPL/MBEFORE/MAFTER control where new content lands relative to what's already there; MCREATE is a separate, independently-set flag controlling where a later create places a new file within a union. Assuming 'appended with -a' also implies 'new files get created here' is wrong — that's MCREATE's job alone, and it's easy to bind something read-only into a union and be surprised when creates keep landing in a different, older element.

A namespace(6) file describes how a name space is built at login/init time, not a live, continuously-enforced policy — bind, mount, and unmount are ordinary system calls any process can call at any later moment. Most real Plan 9 customization (a shell's local rebinding for debugging, iostats wrapping a command's namespace to gather I/O statistics, cpu rebuilding a remote namespace on login) happens by processes mutating their own already-running name space long after boot, not by re-invoking init.

claims.text: Every 9P message begins with a 4-byte size field (the complete message length, including the size field itself), then a 1-byte type (one of the constants in the fcall.h enumeration, e.g. Tversion/Rversion), then a 2-byte tag; the remaining bytes are type-specific parameters. Multi-byte integers are little-endian; variable-length data is a 2-byte count n followed by n bytes; text strings are length-prefixed UTF-8 with no NUL terminator, and the NUL character is illegal in any 9P text field (names, user names, and so on).

A fid is a 32-bit unsigned integer the client chooses to name a "current file" on the server. It is not restricted to files open for I/O — a directory being walked or a file being stat'd is also identified by a fid, so fids cover every file the client is manipulating through the connection. When several independent clients share one connection, whatever agent multiplexes them must ensure no two clients pick the same fid, since all requests on a connection share one fid space.

A qid is the server's own 13-byte identity for a file, independent of any client's fid: a 1-byte type (a bit vector mirroring the high byte of the file's mode — QTDIR, QTAPPEND, QTEXCL, QTAUTH, QTTMP, or QTFILE=0 for a plain file), a 4-byte version that a server typically increments on every modification, and an 8-byte path unique among all files in the server's hierarchy (a file deleted and recreated with the same name must get a different path). Two files on one server hierarchy are the same file if and only if their qids match, and a single client may hold multiple fids that all resolve to one qid.

The 2-byte tag is chosen by the client and echoed unchanged in the server's reply, and it is what makes 9P a genuinely concurrent protocol rather than strict lockstep request/reply: a client may have several T-messages outstanding on one connection at once as long as no two share a tag, and a server is explicitly allowed to delay a reply and answer later-arriving requests first — necessary, for instance, when a pending read is waiting on a synthesized event like a keystroke. The reserved tag NOTAG, (ushort)~0, is used only for the very first Tversion on a connection, before ordinary tag matching applies.

Every T-message's reply is either an R-message whose type is exactly one greater than the request's, or the universal Rerror (there is no per-message error type) carrying an ename string describing the failure — a Tflush is the one exception, since it can never be answered with Rerror.

Tversion/Rversion must be the very first exchange on a fresh connection, using tag NOTAG, and the client may issue no other request until Rversion arrives. The client proposes msize — the largest complete message (including its own 4-byte size field) it will ever send or accept — and a version string that must start with the two characters "9P"; the server replies with its own msize (which must be ≤ the client's) and either the client's version string, an earlier version string it supports instead, or the literal 7-character string "unknown" if it recognizes none of them. A successful version exchange resets the whole connection: all outstanding I/O aborts and every active fid is automatically clunked. The span between one Tversion and the next is called a session.

Authentication in 9P is optional per server and layered on top of the ordinary message set, not a separate channel: Tauth hands the server a fresh afid together with the uname/aname a following Tattach will use. A server that doesn't require authentication just answers Rerror to Tauth, and the client then sets afid to NOFID, (u32int)~0, in Tattach. A server that does require it replies with an aqid of type QTAUTH, which the client reads and writes with ordinary Tread/Twrite messages to run whatever authentication protocol the two sides agree on — 9P itself does not define that protocol. Once it completes, the same validated afid is presented in Tattach to grant entry, and one afid may back multiple attaches sharing that uname/aname.

Tattach is the message that turns a bare connection into a client's view of a tree: it binds a client-chosen fid to the root of the server's exported hierarchy, names the user (uname) and, for servers exporting more than one tree, which one (aname); Rattach's qid is the server's identity for that root. It is an error if fid is already in use. Every later fid on that connection is reached by walking from some already-attached root fid, and every request on it carries the identity established at attach time.

Twalk descends the hierarchy from an existing fid to a new one in a single message, by up to sixteen path elements at once — MAXWELEM, a limit on how many elements one message may carry, not a limit on path depth, since a deeper path simply costs additional Twalk messages. Rwalk carries one qid per successfully walked element, so a partial failure is visible directly in the reply (nwqid less than nwname) without disturbing the original fid or committing newfid; only when nwqid equals nwname does newfid become the file reached by the final element. Walking zero elements makes newfid a duplicate of fid (equivalent to walking to "."), which is how a client clones a fid before using it destructively. ".." is a legal element meaning parent directory (the root's parent is itself); "." is interpreted locally by the client and never appears on the wire.

Topen/Ropen and Tcreate/Rcreate both leave a fid ready for Tread/Twrite and return a qid plus an iounit field that, if nonzero, is the largest transfer guaranteed not to be split across multiple 9P messages. open's 1-byte mode packs an access type — OREAD=0, OWRITE=1, ORDWR=2, OEXEC=3 — with independent bits OTRUNC (0x10, truncate on open) and ORCLOSE (0x40, remove the file when this fid is later clunked); it is illegal to write, truncate, or remove-on-close a directory. create takes a name and requested perm bits (bit 31, DMDIR, requests a directory) that the server masks down against the containing directory's own read/write bits before opening the new file according to mode — so a create that asks for world-readable inside a non-world-readable directory does not get world-readable.

Tread/Rread and Twrite/Rwrite move count bytes at an explicit offset on an already-opened fid — 9P addresses reads and writes by offset directly, closer to pread/pwrite than to a stream the server tracks a cursor for; a Plan 9 seek(2) call moves the client's own notion of offset but generates no 9P message. Reading a directory instead returns a whole number of stat-format directory entries, and a client must resume a directory read exactly at the byte offset the previous read's returned count left off — seeking to any other offset in a directory is illegal.

Tclunk tells the server the client is done with a fid; it does not touch the underlying file unless the fid was opened with ORCLOSE, in which case clunking also removes it. The fid number is immediately reusable in a fresh Twalk or Tattach, and the fid is invalid to the client from that point even if Rclunk itself comes back as an error. Tremove is precisely a clunk with a delete side effect — the server always clunks fid whether or not the removal itself succeeds — and it fails outright if the client lacks write permission in the file's parent directory.

Tstat/Rstat and Twstat/Rwstat move one machine-independent directory-entry structure — housekeeping size/type/dev fields, then qid, mode, atime, mtime, length, and the textual name/uid/gid/muid — the identical structure a directory read returns one of per entry. A wstat request is all-or-nothing (every requested change lands, or none does), and a field can be left untouched explicitly by sending an empty string or the integer field's maximum value; renaming requires write permission in the parent, changing length requires write permission on the file, mode/mtime/gid changes are restricted to the file's owner or the relevant group leader, and nothing in wstat can ever change a file's owner.

Tflush cancels a request still pending under oldtag; the server must answer immediately with Rflush (never Rerror), and either abort the pending transaction or let it run to completion before flushing it. The client must wait for Rflush before reusing oldtag, and — because the flushed request may already have changed server state, e.g. a Tcreate that already created a file or a Twalk that already allocated a fid — if the original reply arrives before the Rflush the client must honor it as having happened rather than as canceled.

Framing on the wire is entirely size-prefixed, not delimiter-based: a message's own leading 4-byte size field is the only thing telling a reader where it ends, so 9P requires a transport that preserves message boundaries and delivers bytes reliably and in order — it has no mechanism of its own to recover from a transmission error. Because raw TCP does not delimit messages and UDP does not guarantee ordered delivery, Plan 9 originally paired 9P with a purpose-built transport, IL (Internet Link), specifically to give it those properties over IP; an implementation running 9P over any byte-stream transport must read exactly size bytes to isolate one message itself.

9P2000 folded together two things an earlier revision of the protocol kept as separate messages. That earlier version paired a session message (a bilateral authentication exchange at connection start) with a clone message (copy an existing fid before walking into a directory, so the directory's own fid survives the walk). 9P2000 splits session's two jobs apart — connection setup and negotiation moves into Tversion, authentication becomes its own optional Tauth exchange — and absorbs clone into Twalk itself, by letting a zero-element walk duplicate a fid and by letting one Twalk carry several path elements at once; a clone-then-several-walks sequence in the older protocol becomes one Twalk message in 9P2000.

9P2000.u is a Unix-oriented dialect negotiated the same way any 9P version is, by proposing a version string such as "9P2000.u" in Tversion; a server that doesn't support it can fall back and answer plain "9P2000", and a well-behaved client degrades to operating without the extension. Where the base protocol identifies users and groups only as text (uname strings), 9P2000.u adds a numeric n_uname field alongside the text fields on attach/auth so a Unix-flavored server can work with numeric uid/gid instead of resolving names; it adds a numeric errno hint field onto Rerror alongside the existing text ename, so a client unable to match the error string can still fall back to a Unix-style numeric error code; and it adds an extension string to the stat/wstat structure so device-special files, symbolic links, and hard links — none of which base 9P2000 has any notion of — can be represented within the existing stat message instead of requiring new message types.

9P2000.L is a separate, larger dialect built specifically to back the Linux VFS — used by Linux's v9fs client and consumed by things like QEMU's virtio-9p transport — rather than an incremental successor to 9P2000.u layering a few extra fields onto the existing message set. It keeps a subset of the 9P2000 core plus 9P2000.u's attach/auth shape, and adds a substantial set of new Linux-shaped message pairs alongside it: Tlopen/Tlcreate (open/create using Linux O_* flags instead of Plan 9's mode byte), Tsymlink, Tmknod, Tlink, Trename/Trenameat, Treadlink, Tgetattr/Tsetattr (a Linux stat(2)-shaped replacement for stat/wstat), Txattrwalk/Txattrcreate, Treaddir, Tfsync, and Tlock/Tgetlock for POSIX advisory locking. Errors on .L are reported through Rlerror, which carries only a numeric Linux errno and no text string at all — the opposite tradeoff from .u's string-plus-numeric-hint approach.

pitfalls: It's easy to assume 9P is strict lockstep request/reply, like a simple RPC call. Tags exist precisely so a client can have multiple T-messages outstanding at once, and a server is explicitly permitted to answer them out of order — code (or a mental model) that assumes replies arrive in the order requests were sent will break against a compliant server.

MAXWELEM (16) is a limit on how many path elements one Twalk message may carry, not a limit on how deep a hierarchy can be — a common misreading. A path sixteen levels deep or deeper is walked by issuing more than one Twalk, transparently, not by hitting a hard ceiling.

Rerror is easy to read as "the operation didn't happen," but Tflush's own semantics contradict that in one specific case: if the original reply to a flushed request arrives before the matching Rflush, the client must honor it as having actually happened — a Tcreate may have already created the file, a Twalk may have already allocated the fid — rather than assume the flush erased the side effect.

Treating 9P2000.u and 9P2000.L as the same idea at two version numbers is a common conflation. They're separate designs for different consumers: .u adds Unix concepts (numeric uid, numeric errno, symlink/device/hardlink support) as extra fields bolted onto the existing 9P2000 messages, while .L instead adds a large parallel set of Linux-VFS-shaped messages (Tlopen, Tgetattr, Tsymlink, and so on) and reports errors with a numeric-only Rlerror — not a superset relationship, and a server speaking one doesn't thereby speak the other.

The version string "9P2000" is easy to treat as synonymous with "9P" the protocol family in general. It's one specific point release negotiated in Tversion; the protocol that preceded it kept authentication (session) and fid-copying (clone) as their own separate message types, which 9P2000 folded into Tversion/Tauth and Twalk respectively — so documentation or wire captures describing the earlier protocol don't map message-for-message onto 9P2000.

claims.text: Every resource in Plan 9 is answered by one of two kinds of 9P server: a kernel device driver, compiled into the kernel and reached through the '#c' bootstrap notation, or a user-level file server, an ordinary process that speaks 9P over a pipe or network connection like any other program. Both implement the identical 13-message protocol; the difference is only where the code that answers those messages runs and how a client gets a channel to it.

A kernel device driver is a 9P server whose messages are dispatched as local procedure calls rather than marshaled onto a wire — no framing, no transport, just a function table the kernel calls directly. Four 9P messages (Nop, Session, Flush, Error) have no subroutine equivalent inside a device driver, because they exist to manage a connection and a device driver has none to manage.

A file name beginning with '#' followed by one device character names the root of the file tree served by that kernel device — e.g. '#c' is the console device, '#p' is the process device, '#s' is the srv registry, '#d' is the fd device. Passing such a name to a system call performs an attach on the corresponding driver; any characters after the device letter but before the next '/' are passed through as the attach's aname (e.g. '#I2' selects IP stack instance 2). This is the one notation that lets a name space be bootstrapped at all, before anything is bound to a conventional path — init(8) uses it, via newns and the namespace(6) file, to bind each device to its conventional location (bind('#c', '/dev', MREPL) is what makes /dev/cons exist) so that ordinary programs afterward never need to know or type a '#' name themselves.

The console device (#c, conventionally bound to /dev) is a representative simple kernel device: a one-level directory of small, independently meaningful files — cons (typed input / console output), consctl (control commands for the console), pid/ppid/pgrpid (identity of the calling process), user, hostowner, time, random, zero, null, reboot — each answering ordinary open/read/write rather than an ioctl-style multiplexed control call.

The process device (#p, conventionally bound to /proc) is a representative two-level kernel device: the top level lists one numbered directory per live pid, and each pid directory exposes files such as ctl, status, mem, fd, ns, note, text, and wait — this is the concrete file tree that lets ps, a debugger, and process control all be plain file I/O instead of dedicated system calls, and it is served by exactly the same 9P mechanism as every remote file server.

A user-level file server built with the C library lib9p (#include <9p.h>) does not hand-roll a read loop: the srv(Srv*) function reads T-messages from an infd, dispatches each to a function pointer in a Srv struct named after the 9P transaction it handles (attach, auth, open, create, read, write, remove, flush, stat, wstat, walk), and writes the R-message to an outfd. A service function must eventually call respond(Req*, char *error) exactly once per request — a nil error string means success — after which the Req and anything it pointed to must be treated as freed.

threadpostmountsrv(Srv*, char *name, char *mtpt, int flag) is the usual way to launch a lib9p server: it allocates a pipe, optionally posts one end at /srv/name via postfd (see srv(3)), forks a child that calls srv() on the other end, and optionally mounts srvfd at mtpt in the caller's own name space — one call does 'start serving, publish it, and graft it into my view,' which is why so many Plan 9 commands (ramfs, exportfs, cdfs, webfs) are small.

lib9p's service loop is explicitly single-threaded and synchronous: while one request is being handled the loop does not read the next, so a slow or blocking service function stalls every other client on the connection. A server that expects some requests to block is expected to hand them to a separate process and let that process call respond() asynchronously later — flush's job is specifically to let a client cancel or hurry along a request left pending that way.

lib9p offers two ways to represent the tree a server exposes. If the Srv has a nonzero tree (a File/Tree hierarchy from the companion 9p-file API — alloctree/createfile/removefile/walkfile/opendirfile), lib9p itself resolves walk, permission-checks open/create/remove/wstat, and serves directory reads, calling into the server's own functions only for read/write/create/remove on actual files — appropriate when the tree is arbitrary and mutable, e.g. ramfs. If tree is left zero, the server must implement its own walk (or hand it to the walkandclone helper with walk1/clone callbacks) and its own directory-read generator (dirread9p) — appropriate when the hierarchy is cheaply computable on demand rather than worth maintaining in memory, e.g. a highly structured, largely fixed layout like cdfs or nntpfs.

The srv device (kernel device #s, conventionally bound to /srv) is a one-level directory that acts as a bulletin board for open file descriptors: a process creates a file such as /srv/name and writes into it the ASCII decimal number of an already-open file descriptor (one end of a pipe to a lib9p server, typically). Any other process can then open /srv/name to get its own reference to that same open file — which is exactly what mount /srv/name /some/point does. The srv entry holds a reference to the file even while no one has it open; removing the entry from /srv releases that reference. Writing more than one number into a server file, or reusing an existing name, is an error.

The srv(4) command line tool (distinct from the srv(3) kernel device, though it uses it) dials a remote 9P service, does the version/attach dance, and posts the resulting connection at /srv/name so any local process can mount it — the 9fs rc(1) script wraps srv plus a conventional mount onto /n/system in one step, which is the ordinary way a Plan 9 user reaches another machine's files.

exportfs is the standard user-level answer to 'let a remote machine see part of my name space' without any special network file-system protocol: it is itself a 9P server, but instead of a File tree backed by real storage, every operation it receives is re-executed as an ordinary system call against the local name space it was started in, and the result relayed back over the wire. The cpu(1) command is exportfs's canonical use — a cpu server dials back to the user's terminal, runs exportfs there, and mounts the result on /mnt/term, so device files that only make sense on the terminal (the console, the mouse) remain reachable from processes actually executing on the (faster) compute server.

consolefs is a compact worked example of good file-server interface design: a single lib9p process presents each configured console as up to three small files (console, consolectl, consolestat) rather than one file overloaded with an ioctl-style side channel, broadcasts console output to every reader that has it open (so a shared serial line behaves like a shared terminal), and announces every open/close of a console to the other readers as a bracketed text line — the entire access-control and multi-reader-notification policy is expressed as file content and file structure, not as new system calls.

A recurring design idiom across Plan 9 file servers is the ctl/data (or name / namectl) file pair: a plain data file carries the payload (console bytes, network bytes, a console's data), while a same-named-plus-'ctl' file accepts short text commands that change how the data file behaves — /net/tcp/n/{data,ctl}, /dev/{cons,consctl}, /mnt/consoles/{name,namectl} in consolefs all follow it. The convention keeps every server's control surface readable and writable with cat/echo instead of a bespoke ioctl-equivalent, and it is precisely the mechanism chapter 1 pointed at when it said Plan 9 routes control operations themselves through ordinary file I/O.

Good file-server interface design, as the primary sources model it, has a consistent shape: expose one small, stable directory per logical resource; give control its own separate file rather than overloading the data file's semantics; let names — not new operation codes — be where a design decision shows up (a numbered connection directory, a per-pid directory, a per-console directory); and choose the File/Tree API only when the tree is genuinely dynamic, otherwise generate it on the fly, because a generated tree needs no memory management and cannot drift out of sync with whatever it's a view of.

snippets.note: Trimmed from 9p(3)'s Srv struct and function synopsis — the shape every lib9p server (ramfs, cdfs, webfs, …) fills in.

snippets.code:
% bind -a '#t' /dev      # graft the serial-port device's root into /dev
% bind '#c'    /dev      # the console device — what init does for you at boot
% bind '#p'    /proc     # the process device
% bind '#s'    /srv      # the srv registry itself is a device, too
snippets.note: The '#'-device bootstrap notation from intro(3); init(8) performs the conventional ones automatically from namespace(6) so ordinary programs never type a '#' name.
srv(3)'s own example of posting an open fd and a second process picking it up via mount — the mechanism srv(4)/9fs and threadpostmountsrv build on.

pitfalls: It's easy to read 'kernel device' and 'file server' as different mechanisms. They're the same 9P interface implemented at two different distances: a device driver answers 9P messages as local procedure calls with no wire at all, a user-level server answers the identical messages read off a pipe or network connection — attach, walk, open, read all mean exactly the same thing either way, which is precisely what lets bind and mount treat both uniformly.

The '#' device notation looks like a special case bolted onto the namespace, but it is the opposite: it is the one thing that makes the namespace bootstrappable at all before any conventional bind has happened. Assuming ordinary programs use '#c' or '#p' directly is a common misreading — by the time a shell prompt appears, init has already bound every conventional device via namespace(6), and typing a raw '#' name in rc even requires quoting to escape the shell's own comment character.

srv(3) the kernel device (the /srv registry mechanism: create a file, write an fd number into it) is easy to conflate with srv(4) the command-line tool (dial a remote machine, then use the srv(3) mechanism to post the resulting connection). They're layered, not synonyms — srv(4) and threadpostmountsrv both use the srv(3) device, but plenty of code posts to /srv directly without going through either.

A File/Tree-backed server is not automatically the right choice. lib9p's tree support (createfile/walkfile/etc.) exists for hierarchies that are genuinely maintained in memory and mutate over time; a server whose tree is easily regenerated on demand (cdfs listing tracks, nntpfs listing newsgroups) is explicitly better off leaving tree nil and implementing walk/dirread9p itself — reaching for File/Tree by default adds reference-counted memory management (9p-file(3) itself calls it 'cumbersome') a generated tree doesn't need.

The lib9p service loop is single-threaded by design, not by oversight — a service function that blocks (waiting on real I/O, a lock, another process) stalls every other pending request on that connection. Writing a slow operation directly into a service function, instead of handing it to a helper process that calls respond() later, is a real way to make an otherwise-correct file server feel hung under load.

claims.text: bind and mount both modify the file name space of the current process and other processes in its name-space group. For both calls, old names an existing file or directory already in the current name space; it is evaluated as in intro(2), except the final path element is not translated (so old itself, not what it currently points to, is the thing being changed).

Both bind and mount take a flag governing how the newly-visible thing joins whatever is already at old. MREPL (the default, value 0) replaces old outright; if the result is a directory (for mount this is true by definition, since a mount target must be a directory) old becomes a union directory of exactly one component, the new one. MBEFORE requires both old and the new thing to be directories and splices the new directory onto the front of the union at old, so it is searched first. MAFTER is identical but splices onto the end. MCREATE can be OR'd onto any of MREPL/MBEFORE/MAFTER to mark that specific component as eligible to receive a newly created file. MCACHE, valid only for mount, turns on local client-side caching for files reached through that mount; by default file contents are always fetched fresh from the server, and with MCACHE on, currency of a cached file is re-verified at each open, not on every read.

At the command line, bind(1) and mount(1) expose the same flags as options: no option is MREPL, -b is MBEFORE, -a is MAFTER, -c is MCREATE (usable with either -b or -a, or alone), and -C (mount only) is MCACHE. mount also takes -k keypattern to constrain which factotum(4) key is used and -n to skip authentication entirely; -q makes either command exit silently on failure. The namespace(6) description-file operations mount and bind accept the identical option letters, interpreted exactly as in bind(1).

A union directory is what results when bind or mount stacks multiple directories at one point in the name space; Plan 9 documentation describes it as behaving like the concatenation of its constituent directories. A file-name lookup in a union directory searches each component in the union's order and takes the first match; reading a union directory (e.g. via ls) likewise concatenates the directory listing of each component in that same order.

The canonical union directory is /bin itself: it is built as a union of /$cputype/bin (the compiled binaries for the local architecture) and /rc/bin (architecture-independent shell scripts), plus optionally more directories a user adds. Because the search order is structural — part of the name space, not a per-shell variable — this construction makes the shell's $PATH variable unnecessary; Plan 9's rc has no such variable at all.

Which union component receives a newly-created file is governed separately from lookup order. By default, a directory added to a union does not accept new files at all, though create() on a name that already exists in that directory still succeeds normally regardless of the flag. The MCREATE flag, set when a directory is bound or mounted into the union, marks that component as create-eligible. When create() makes a genuinely new name inside a union directory, the components are tried in union order and the file is created in the first one that has create permission; if that particular create fails (e.g. no write permission), the whole create() fails — it does not fall through to try the next create-eligible component.

This creation rule is deliberately designed to support one common pattern: a user unions a private, writable directory into an otherwise public, read-only union (for example, ahead of /bin with -b -c) so that new files they create land in their own directory while the public components stay untouched.

Internally, the kernel represents the whole name space as a mount table: a list of (from, to) channel pairs. Whenever a walk successfully advances a channel to a new name, the mount table is checked for a from entry matching that name; if one exists, the to channel is cloned and substituted for the channel the walk was using. A union directory is implemented by making that to channel the head of a linked list of channels, one per union component. If a walk fails to find the requested name in the first channel of the list, it follows the list, clones the next channel, and retries the walk there — which is the mechanical, per-name-lookup version of the 'search each component in order, first match wins' rule.

unmount(char *name, char *old) reverses a bind or mount. If name is the null string/zero, everything currently bound or mounted at old is removed — the whole union at that point, however many components it has. If name is non-zero, it is evaluated exactly as bind's name argument is, and only the binding that would attach that specific result to old is undone, leaving any other components of a union at old untouched.

mount(2) documents a specific ordering constraint as a BUGS-section note: mount does not return until it has successfully attached to the file server, so the process performing the mount cannot simultaneously be the process serving the connection — posting the pipe end for serving and mounting the other end must happen from separate processes (or the server side must already be running before the mount call).

The namespace(6) description-file format and the ns(1) command (already introduced as the mechanism that boots a process's first name space and inspects a running one) are the same vocabulary this chapter's flags feed into: every mount/bind line in a namespace(6) file, and every line ns(1) prints back from /proc/pid/ns, is exactly one of these bind(2)/mount(2) calls with one of these four flags, spelled out as its bind(1)/mount(1) option letters.

snippets.note: flag constants and signatures per bind(2)/mount(2); MREPL/MBEFORE/MAFTER are mutually exclusive positions, MCREATE and MCACHE are independent bits OR'd onto any of them

snippets.code:
# /bin as a union: architecture binaries, then rc scripts, then a private directory
bind -a /386/bin  /bin      # -a = MAFTER: append at the end of the union
bind -a /rc/bin   /bin      # -a = MAFTER: append after that
bind -b -c $home/bin /bin   # -b -c = MBEFORE|MCREATE: search ME first, and
                             #   anything I create lands here, not in /bin's
                             #   public components
snippets.note: option letters and semantics per bind(1); /$cputype/bin + /rc/bin union per the overview paper's description of /bin

snippets.code:
# undo one specific binding vs. undo everything at a point
unmount /n/dump/1992/0716/mips/lib/libc.a /mips/lib/libc.a   # undo just this bind
unmount /mips/lib/libc.a                                      # undo EVERYTHING bound/mounted there
snippets.note: two-argument vs. one-argument unmount per bind(1)/bind(2)

pitfalls: MCREATE marks a component eligible to receive new files; it does not make that component the exclusive target. Creation of a genuinely new name still walks the union in search order (as fixed by MBEFORE/MAFTER placement) and uses the first component with create permission — order and MCREATE interact, neither alone determines where a file lands.

MCREATE only affects create() of a name that does not yet exist anywhere in the union. create() on a name that already exists in some (non-create-eligible) component succeeds normally through ordinary open-for-write semantics — a union with no MCREATE component at all is not read-only for files that are already there, only for genuinely new names.

unmount with a single argument removes every component bound or mounted at that point, not just the most recently added one — the natural-looking 'undo my last bind' call is actually the two-argument form naming exactly what to remove.

MBEFORE/MAFTER require both old and the incoming name to already be directories; you cannot union two plain files, and mount's target must always be a directory since the served tree's root is grafted there.

A union directory's concatenation is positional shadowing, not merging: if the same file name exists in two components, only the first (search-order) match is reachable by that name — the second component's file of the same name is simply never seen through that name, it does not overlay or combine with it.

claims.text: rfork is the only mechanism Plan 9 has for creating new processes; fork() is defined as nothing more than the fixed call rfork(RFFDG|RFREND|RFPROC). Rfork takes a single int flag argument, a bit vector, and each resource it governs -- the file name space, the open file descriptor table, environment variables, the note group, and (via RFMEM) data/bss memory segments -- is shared identically between parent and child by default; each has its own bit(s) to instead copy it independently or, for several, start it empty.

RFPROC decides whether rfork creates a new process at all. If set, a child process is created: the parent's rfork returns the child's pid, the child's returns 0. If RFPROC is not set, none of the other bits create anything -- they modify the resources of the calling process itself, in place. rfork(RFNAMEG) alone, with no RFPROC, is a complete and legal call: it detaches the calling process's own name space from whoever it was sharing with, without forking.

RFFDG causes the invoker's open file descriptor table to be copied into the child as an independent table, though the descriptors in that new table still refer to the very same open channels the parent had open at the moment of the call -- it is the small-integer-to-channel mapping that becomes independent, not the underlying files. Without RFFDG, parent and child share one table outright: closing a descriptor in either process closes it for both, and either process opening a new file changes what the other sees at that descriptor number too. RFCFDG instead gives the child a table with nothing open in it. A descriptor table, shared or copied, stays open only until it is explicitly closed or every process sharing it has exited.

Environment variables are themselves a kernel file device, #e, conventionally bound to /env, with one file per variable holding its value as text. Under a plain fork(), parent and child continue to see exactly the same /env files -- a change made through either process's environment is visible to the other, mirroring the shared-by-default name-space behavior of a plain fork. RFENVG splits that: both process groups start from an identical set of files, but a subsequent change in one is no longer visible to the other. RFCENVG splits and also clears, so the child starts with no environment variables at all.

RFMEM shares the data and bss memory segments between parent and child outright, instead of the child receiving its own copy of those segments; the stack segment is unaffected by RFMEM and is always given to the child as a copy-on-write fork regardless of which flags are passed. RFMEM may be set only together with RFPROC -- it has no meaning as an in-place modification of a single already-running process, only as a property of a newly created one.

Plan 9 deliberately has one class of process, not a split between heavyweight processes and lightweight kernel threads as other systems of the era were adding; rfork's bit vector gives fine, independent control over which resources -- name space, environment, descriptor table, memory, notes -- are shared, copied, or started clean, so the same primitive covers everything from a plain fork() to something close to a shared-memory thread. The design paper notes that, apart from the library's own fork(), it is hard to find two rfork call sites in Plan 9 that pass the same bits: programs use it to build many distinct shapes of sharing rather than choosing between exactly two.

The process device (conventionally bound as #p /proc) serves a two-level directory: a flat top level of numbered directories, one per live local process named by its pid, plus one extra file, /proc/trace, for cross-process trace events. Each per-pid directory exposes files including mem, text, ctl, status, note, notepg, noteid, fd, ns, wait, args, regs, fpregs, kregs, segment, and profile, each read or written as plain text or a small fixed binary format rather than through a dedicated system call -- the same file-I/O interface the rest of Plan 9 uses for every other resource.

The read-only ns file in each /proc/pid directory holds a textual reconstruction of that process's file name space, written in the same namespace(6) syntax that newns/addns consume to build a name space in the first place, with a final cd line giving the process's current working directory. Its contents are based on the names files had at the moment each piece of the name space was assembled, not looked up fresh when ns is read, so if a bound file was later renamed or moved, the script ns prints can no longer accurately rebuild that name space.

Textual messages written to a process's ctl file control its execution without any ptrace-equivalent system call: stop suspends it into the Stopped state, start resumes a Stopped process, kill marks it to be killed the next time it crosses into the kernel, close n and closefiles close one or all of its open file descriptors, private makes its user memory unreadable by any other process (inherited on fork, cleared on exec), and pri n sets its base scheduling priority; waitstop/startstop additionally block the writer until the target reaches the Stopped state or exits.

note and notepg are the two write targets for sending a process a note (Plan 9's analog of a UNIX signal): a string written to note is posted to that one process only, while the same string written to notepg is delivered to every process in the target's note group -- the set of processes that, per RFNOTEG in rfork(2), share a note group -- except that a process which writes to its own notepg does not itself receive the note back. noteid, also under /proc/pid, is a readable/writable integer identifying which note group a process currently belongs to.

/proc is a deliberately restrained abstraction: it is only a view onto an existing process's state, never a way to create or fully become one. The Plan 9 designers explicitly reject tricks like cp /bin/date /proc/clone/mem as a way to spawn a process by writing to /proc, because doing so would require the file server answering /proc's 9P requests to take actions -- constructing a new process's open files, name space, and memory image -- that do not fall naturally out of ordinary read/write/create semantics. Process creation stays on the conventional rfork/exec path; /proc only represents and controls processes that already exist.

Per-process device instances are not a special kernel feature bolted onto specific files -- they fall out of ordinary name-space mechanics. The window system (8½) is itself a user-level file server for files including /dev/cons and /dev/bitblt; each client window mounts its own connection to 8½ into its private name space, so there are simultaneously many distinct instances of a file literally named /dev/cons, one per window, each served independently by 8½. A process's standard input, output, and error are simply connected to whichever /dev/cons its own name space resolves that name to. This contrasts with UNIX's /dev/tty, which is implemented by special kernel code that overloads the file, on open, with whichever terminal happens to be attached to the calling process -- on Plan 9 the same effect is ordinary namespace binding, with no special-casing needed in the kernel at all.

Plan 9 has no mechanism to hand the description of one process's name space to another process except by direct inheritance through fork/rfork -- there is no operation to export a running namespace as data. The cpu command, which recreates a terminal's environment on a remote CPU server, cannot literally reproduce the terminal's current name space; it can only re-interpret the user's login profile and substitute a few conventional pieces such as the binary directory for the CPU server's own architecture, which misses any local, ad hoc modifications the user made to their name space before invoking cpu.

snippets.note: flag semantics per fork(2)/rfork(2); RFNAMEG/RFCNAMEG were already introduced in chapter 2 -- shown here only for the shared-vs-copy-vs-clean pattern

snippets.code:
# inspect and control process 17 through plain files, no ptrace anywhere
cat  /proc/17/status                  # name, state, cpu time, priority...
cat  /proc/17/ns                      # its namespace, as namespace(6) text
echo stop  >/proc/17/ctl              # suspend it
echo note!hello >/proc/17/note        # post a note to just this process
echo hello >/proc/17/notepg           # post the same note to its whole note group
snippets.note: ctl/status/ns/note/notepg per proc(3); the ns file's format is namespace(6), the same vocabulary chapter 2 covered

pitfalls: Plain fork() does NOT isolate a child's name space, environment, or file descriptor table -- the un-flagged default for all three is share, not copy. RFNAMEG/RFENVG/RFFDG are what you pass to get independence; this is the same shared-by-default pattern chapter 2 already established for name spaces specifically, and it holds for environment and descriptors too.

RFFDG copies the descriptor *table*, not the files it points to: after the copy, descriptor 3 in the child still refers to the exact same open channel descriptor 3 referred to in the parent. What becomes independent is only the mapping from small integers to those channels (e.g. later opens/closes in one process no longer affect the other's numbering).

RFMEM only shares data and bss. The stack is always forked copy-on-write regardless of any flag, and RFMEM is meaningless (an error) unless combined with RFPROC -- it describes a property of a newly created process, not an in-place change to the caller.

There is no way to spawn a process by writing to /proc (e.g. no /proc/clone the way some systems' pseudo-filesystems allow); /proc is read/inspect/control only, and process creation always goes through rfork and exec.

The ns file is not a live, re-resolved view -- it reports the names a process's name space was built from at assembly time. If something it names was since renamed or removed, the reconstruction ns prints is stale and may no longer produce the same name space if replayed.

A process cannot capture and hand off an exact copy of its current name space to an unrelated process (e.g. over the network via cpu) -- only direct fork/rfork inheritance carries a name space forward faithfully; everything else (like cpu re-running a login profile) only approximates the original.

claims.text: Plumbing is an inter-process communication mechanism for passing messages between interactive programs as part of the Plan 9 user interface; its core is a language-driven file server, the plumber, which receives, examines, rewrites, and dispatches messages according to configurable pattern-action rules rather than requiring the user to manually carry data between programs (as with cut-and-paste or drag-and-drop).

Programs send messages by writing to the file /mnt/plumb/send, and receive messages by reading from 'ports' — other files served under /mnt/plumb, such as /mnt/plumb/edit, which by convention is where text editors read requests to open and display a file.

A plumb message has a fixed-format textual header of six lines, in order — src (source application), dst (destination port), wdir (working directory, used to resolve relative filenames), type (a MIME-like tag such as text; only type=text is currently supported), attr (blank-separated name=value attribute pairs, quoted per rc(1) conventions), and ndata (the byte length of what follows) — followed by a free-format data section with no terminating newline; only the data section may itself contain embedded newlines, and all header fields are optional except that ndata must be an accurate count.

The C library represents a message as struct Plumbmsg { char *src, *dst, *wdir, *type; Plumbattr *attr; int ndata; char *data; }, with struct Plumbattr { char *name, *value; Plumbattr *next; } as a linked list of attributes; plumb(2) provides plumbopen/plumbsend/plumbrecv/plumbpack/plumbunpack and attribute helpers (plumblookup, plumbaddattr, plumbdelattr) to build, transmit, and parse messages without hand-rolling the wire format.

Plumbing rules are read from a rules file (default $home/lib/plumbing) written in a small pattern-action language: the file is a sequence of blank-line-separated rule sets, each containing one or more one-line patterns followed by one or more one-line actions; lines starting with # are comments; an `include file` line splices in a shared rule fragment, searched first relative to the plumber's own directory and then in /sys/lib/plumb.

Every rule — pattern or action — has the shape 'object verb [arguments]'. Pattern objects are message fields (src, dst, wdir, type, data, attr) or arg (the rule's own argument); pattern verbs include is (exact match), isdir (object names an existing directory; sets $dir), isfile (object names an existing file; sets $file), and matches (regex match against the argument; sets $0, $1, ... to the whole match and parenthesized submatches). Rewriting verbs — add and delete (on attr) and set (assign a field) — always succeed and permanently modify the message, so they belong after the matching patterns in a rule set. Action rules always have object plumb, with exactly three verbs: to (name a destination port), client (start a command and hold the message for delivery once that command opens the port), and start (start a command and discard the message).

Rule sets are tried in file order against an incoming message; the first rule set whose patterns all succeed is triggered and the rest are ignored for that message. If no rule set matches, the message is rejected — the write to /mnt/plumb/send fails, so the sending program can detect the failure — unless the message already names an existing destination port in its dst field, in which case it is emitted there unchanged.

The click attribute (a numeric cursor offset within the data, set by the sending program) switches `data matches` rules from requiring a match of the whole string to finding the longest leftmost regular-expression match that touches the click position; when several `matches` rules appear in one rule set, each must match the identical substring for the set to succeed, which is how a broad rule (extract plausible filename characters) combined with a narrower one (require a known image-file suffix) avoids misreading text like 'horse.gift' as the file 'horse.gif'. Once click has been used to narrow the data this way, the plumber deletes the click attribute from the outgoing message.

Output ports are created dynamically: the set of ports is exactly the set of unique port names appearing in `plumb to` actions across the active rules. Once created, a port is never deleted — even if a later rules-file edit removes every rule that named it, the port persists (though nothing will deliver to it anymore).

The plumber's ruleset is itself a live, editable file: reading /mnt/plumb/rules returns the text of the currently active rules; appending to it adds a new rule set immediately, with no restart; opening it with truncation (O_TRUNC) clears the rule set entirely. This lets an operator change plumbing behavior on a running system with an ordinary text editor.
The plumber implements fan-out delivery: if multiple client programs have the same destination port open for reading, each receives its own independent copy of a message sent to that port.

Message delivery from send to a port is intentionally non-blocking and best-effort rather than guaranteed: a write to /mnt/plumb/send succeeds as soon as the message is queued for its destination, not once a reader actually consumes it, so the sender is never blocked waiting on a slow or absent recipient — but a message can silently fail to arrive, for example if the intended reader process exits while messages are still queued for it. The design explicitly favors this non-blocking property over delivery reliability, since plumbing serves the interactive user interface rather than acting as a general reliable IPC channel.

The plumb(1) shell command sends a message from the command line or a script, e.g. `plumb mem.c`; flags set the message fields explicitly (-s source, -d destination, -t type, -a attributes, -w working directory, -p an alternate plumb file), and -i reads the data from standard input instead of the argument list, in which case plumb adds an action=showdata attribute by default if none was given.

Canonical worked example from the design paper: a user points at the string 'rmstar.c:32:' printed by a failed compile in a terminal window and invokes the plumb action; the terminal emulator sends that string as a message. A rule set splits it into a filename and a line number, confirms rmstar.c exists as a file in the message's wdir, rewrites the message's data to just 'rmstar.c', attaches an addr=32 attribute, and dispatches it to the edit port; the already-running text editor receives it and jumps straight to line 32.

Acme's right-button 'acquire' feature is implemented on top of the plumber: right-clicking a piece of text has Acme construct a plumbing message from the whitespace-delimited text around the click (using the click attribute) and write it to send; if that write fails, Acme falls back to its own built-in behavior (a context search within the current document). Other Plan 9 programs — sam's plumb menu entry, the faces mail-monitor program, the edmail reader — are plumbing clients in the same way, letting components with very different user interfaces interoperate through one shared bus.

Because the plumber is an ordinary Plan 9 file server rather than a kernel facility or a bespoke RPC layer, plumbing messages cross the network exactly like any other file operation: a window system and the applications it talks to can live on different machines yet still share one plumber instance transparently, and the plumber's service is additionally published through srv(4) (named by $plumbsrv) so it can be mounted elsewhere. Ordinary file permissions are the plumber's only access control — no special authentication layer is added on top.

A `plumb start` action always runs its command and discards the triggering message (fire-and-forget); a `plumb client` action runs its command but retains the message, delivering it to that program once the program itself opens the named destination port — used when the started program needs the message's structured fields (such as an addr attribute), not just a bare filename on its command line. Only one start or client action should appear per rule set, and the `plumb to` action is evaluated out of the usual pattern order: if the incoming message already names a dst port, a rule set only matches when its own `plumb to` names that same port.

The plumbing system's own architecture is deliberately unusual for two reasons the design paper argues are advantages: rules are described in a small language rather than compiled into applications, so behavior can be added or changed without rebuilding or restarting anything; and the plumber is a file server, so no additional IPC technology (remote procedure call, message brokers) is needed to make it work — plumbing reuses the read/write operations and network transparency every Plan 9 file service already has.

The plumber's own known limitation, noted in its manual page: its file name space is effectively fixed once it starts running, so it is difficult to correctly plumb messages that refer to files under services mounted into the namespace after the plumber began executing.
