pitfalls: Plumbing is not a clipboard or an explicit send-to-X mechanism — the user never names a recipient; the plumber decides the destination purely from the message's content and the active rules, which surprises readers expecting cut-and-paste semantics.

A single broad `data matches` pattern with no confirming second pattern can misfire on near-miss text (the design paper's own example: 'horse.gift' looking like the image file 'horse.gif') — correct rules pair a loose extraction pattern with a stricter verification pattern that must match the same substring.

Delivery from send is fire-and-queue, not fire-and-confirm: a program can believe a message was delivered successfully (the write succeeded) even though the intended reader later exits without ever consuming it — there is no acknowledgment of actual receipt, only of queuing.

`plumb start` and `plumb client` are easy to swap by mistake: `start` discards the message after launching the command (fine for a self-sufficient command), while `client` is required whenever the launched program needs the message's own fields (e.g. an address) rather than just a bare filename argument — using `start` where `client` was needed silently drops that data.

The plumber's namespace is fixed at the point it starts running (documented as a BUG in plumber(4)), so services mounted afterward are not reliably reachable by rules that reference their files — a real, acknowledged limitation, not an oversight to explain away.

claims.text: Plan 9 has no privileged superuser analogous to Unix root. The closest analogue is the host owner: the user id that initially owns a machine's local resources — the scheduler, local disks, network interfaces. On a single-user machine (a terminal) the host owner is simply that user; a shared machine such as a CPU or file server normally starts with a pseudo-user as host owner. Unlike root, the host owner has no privileges hardcoded into the kernel — it is described explicitly as 'just a regular user that happens to own the resources of the local machine,' so what looks like privilege is a starting allocation of ownership, not a special kernel-enforced role.

Plan 9 has no setuid mechanism. A new process always runs as the same user id as the process that created it — there is no equivalent of an executable bit that changes the running uid on exec. A process instead changes its user id only by proving its right to do so through an explicit, kernel-mediated capability exchange brokered by factotum (see the capability device, below). The security paper draws the contrast directly: were factotum's capability device available on Unix, 'programs like su and login would no longer need to be installed "setuid root."'

factotum is a single per-user agent process that holds a copy of the user's keys and negotiates every authentication protocol on the user's behalf; no other program contains cryptographic code. It is implemented, like most Plan 9 services, as an ordinary file server, conventionally mounted at /mnt/factotum. Concentrating security code in one place buys: applications no longer need cryptographic code (and so can run at lower privilege); a broken or obsolete protocol is fixed by updating factotum alone, not every program that used it; keys for every service are managed uniformly; and unmodified legacy applications get single sign-on for free, since factotum — not the application — does the prompting.

factotum presents a small, fixed set of files at its mountpoint: rpc (each open is a private conversation channel to factotum), ctl (write key/delkey commands; reading it lists current keys, showing only public attributes), proto (lists supported protocols), confirm and needkey (hooks for a GUI to approve sensitive key use or supply a missing key interactively), and log (a debugging trace). File permissions on these — rpc is world read/write, but ctl/confirm/needkey/log are owner-only — are the entire access-control layer; nothing about factotum's protocol requires a separate authorization check.

A factotum key is a set of attribute=value pairs — e.g. proto=p9sk1 user=gre !password='...' — stored and displayed as plain UTF-8 text rather than a binary or certificate format, a deliberate choice the paper justifies on the grounds that text is something a user can actually read, audit, and understand, unlike, say, the contents of an X.509 certificate. An attribute name prefixed with ! is secret: factotum will never print its value and never lets it leave its own address space, with a single narrow exception (the plaintext-password protocol, proto=pass, whose entire job is to disclose user/!password). A program selects a key with a query — a list of attribute=value pairs (exact match) and/or attribute? terms (existence match) — and a key matches only if every query term is satisfied.

Authentication in 9P is layered on the ordinary message set, not baked into the protocol: Tauth hands the server a fresh afid for the uname/aname a later Tattach will use, and (per the 9P chapter) a server that requires authentication replies with an aqid of type QTAUTH which the client reads and writes with plain Tread/Twrite to run whichever protocol the two factotums agree on — 9P itself never defines that protocol, so it can change without touching 9P's spec. The user-level fauth(int fd, char *servicename) system call requests this authentication file directly; once the exchange over it succeeds, the same file descriptor (afd) is presented to mount as proof of identity — afd behaves like a capability: it can be handed to another process, held for later reuse, or closed to revoke it.

amount() is the library routine most programs call instead of raw fauth+mount: it calls fauth to get an afd, runs auth_proxy(afd, getkey, "proto=p9any role=client") to let factotum negotiate and validate over that file descriptor, then calls mount with the (now validated) afd, and closes it. auth_proxy's fmt argument is a factotum key query — 'proto=p9any role=client' asks factotum to run the p9any negotiation metaprotocol as the client role; a getkey callback function is invoked only if factotum needs secret material (a password, a challenge response) it doesn't already hold.

p9any is a small negotiation metaprotocol, used by every native Plan 9 service, that lets the two ends pick which underlying authentication protocol to run without either side hardcoding it: the callee sends a version number plus a list of proto@domain choices for which its factotum holds a key; the caller responds with the one it chooses; the callee confirms with a fixed-length OK, after which the chosen protocol runs. A man-in-the-middle can only narrow the callee's advertised choices, not force either side onto a protocol it wasn't already willing to use — an accepted, bounded weakness rather than a full break.

The Plan 9 shared-key protocol p9sk1 is a Kerberos-style ticket protocol (its tickets substitute a random nonce and counter for Kerberos's expiration time) run between the two factotums and a trusted authentication server: the AS issues a pair of tickets, one encrypted in the client's key and one in the server's, wrapping a fresh shared secret; each side proves knowledge of that secret with an authenticator built from the exchanged nonce, convincing the other of its identity. A successful run of p9sk1 (or any of factotum's shared-key/challenge-response protocols) can additionally hand the server a capability, described next, that lets it actually become the authenticated user.

A kernel device — reached via #¤ and conventionally exposing /dev/caphash and /dev/capuse — lets a trusted process empower another process to change its own user id, without any setuid bit anywhere. A capability is the string old-user@new-user@random-key. The trusted process (in practice, factotum, running as host owner) computes an SHA1-HMAC of old-user@new-user keyed by random-key and writes that 20-byte hash to caphash — a write-only file the host owner may open exactly once, immediately after boot. It then hands the full capability string to the process (already running as old-user) that should become new-user. That process writes the capability string to capuse; the kernel recomputes the hash, looks for a match in its list, and if found changes the writing process's user id to new-user. A capability is single-use: the kernel discards the matching hash once it's consumed, or after roughly a minute if it's never used. Capabilities are purely local to the kernel that issued them — a factotum on one machine cannot mint a capability usable on another.

auth_chuid(AuthInfo *ai, char *ns) is the library call that performs the capuse side of a capability exchange on behalf of a server program: given the AuthInfo (containing the cap field, a capability string) that auth_proxy returned after a successful server-role authentication, auth_chuid writes it to capuse and the process's uid changes to the authenticated client's. This is exactly how, for example, a login service on a shared CPU server, running initially as the host owner, becomes the actual logging-in user only after that user has proved their identity to the host owner's factotum — no setuid binary, no root-owned helper, just an authenticated handoff through the capability device.

Because factotum holds every user's secrets in its own memory, Plan 9 hardens the one remaining leak path — another process reading factotum's state through /proc. Writing private to a process's own /proc/pid/ctl makes that process's memory unreadable through /proc by any other process, even one owned by the same user (it is inherited across fork and cleared on exec); writing noswap keeps its memory pages from ever being written to a swap device, where they could later be recovered. factotum issues both to itself at startup. Neither control message is factotum-specific — any process handling sensitive in-memory state (the paper names dossrv's FAT filesystem buffer cache as another example) can use the same two messages.

factotum's own keys must come from somewhere at boot, before any authenticated channel exists to fetch them securely — this is what secstore solves. secstore is a separate network file server, used only during bootstrap, that stores a user's permanent key file encrypted under a password, protected end-to-end by PAK (a password-authenticated Diffie-Hellman key-exchange protocol chosen for having a strength-equivalence proof), which gives mutual authentication and resists both passive eavesdropping and offline dictionary attacks on the password. Once factotum has fetched and decrypted the key file at login, ordinary encrypted/authenticated file access takes over for everything else — secstore's job ends at bootstrap.

Plan 9's security design is best read as namespace design rather than as a bolt-on permission system: because virtually every resource — a device, a network connection, another process's state, a remote file tree — is reached exclusively through whatever is bound or mounted into a process's private namespace (established in earlier chapters, including RFNOMNT's ability to forbid further mounts and '#'-device dereferencing in a restricted namespace), constraining what appears in that namespace is itself a form of access control, achieved with the same bind/mount/rfork primitives used for ordinary customization rather than a separate mechanism. The conventional file-permission bits (owner/group/other rwx) on whatever is actually reached through that namespace remain the other, more familiar layer — and 9P structurally forecloses at least one classic privilege-escalation path itself: wstat can never change a file's owner, no matter who calls it.

The paper's own stated goal, restated in its conclusion, is to shrink the amount of code that must be trusted with high privilege down to a single, auditable component: factotum's core is a few thousand lines, verifiable by manual or automated means, rather than requiring every network-facing server to separately get its cryptographic code right while running with the privileges needed to use it. Because factotum is the only process that ever creates a capability, every other network service can run as an unprivileged pseudo-user (Plan 9's none, analogous to Unix's nobody) — so a compromised, buggy server has nothing privileged to hand an attacker.

pitfalls: Reading 'host owner' as Plan 9's root is a natural but wrong translation. It carries no kernel-enforced special powers at all — it is an ordinary user id that starts out owning local resources at boot; the paper is explicit that it is 'far weaker' than root precisely because nothing privileged is hardcoded to that identity.

It's tempting to credit factotum itself with the power to change a process's user id. It doesn't — factotum can only authenticate and, on success, obtain a capability from the kernel; the actual uid change happens only when some process writes that capability to /dev/capuse, a kernel operation factotum merely triggers by being the (sole, host-owner-only) writer of /dev/caphash.

Capabilities minted by /dev/caphash are easy to assume are portable credentials, like a Kerberos ticket. They are strictly local to the kernel that created the matching hash entry — a factotum on one machine has no way to produce a capability a different machine's kernel will honor.

Because Tauth/afid already appeared in the 9P chapter as wire mechanics, it's easy to assume 9P itself defines an authentication algorithm. It deliberately doesn't: the afid is just a file that ordinary Tread/Twrite move bytes through, and what those bytes mean is a private agreement between the two factotums (p9sk1, p9any, apop, ...) — which is exactly why Plan 9 has changed its authentication protocols repeatedly without ever revising 9P's spec.

Assuming /proc access is already locked down by ordinary file permissions is only half right: default /proc permissions do stop a different user from reading a process's memory, but they do nothing against another process running as the *same* user — that gap is what the private control message exists specifically to close, and it's opt-in, not automatic, for any process (including factotum) that wants it.
